title: Bowen 'failed Australians' at COP31, Deputy Opposition Leader says
transcript:
Host: There are several key issues the Parliament is dealing with as it sits for this final week of the year. Jane Hume is the deputy opposition leader and Shadow Minister for employment and industrial relations. I spoke to her a little earlier.
Host: Jane Hume, welcome back to Radio National Breakfast.
Jane Hume: Good to be with you, Sally.
Host: Let's talk about COP 31. Countries have walked away from the talks into care without a deal. What's your reaction to that?
Jane Hume: Well, it's extraordinary, isn't it? I mean, we spend $150 million to make Chris Bowen co-president and indeed lead negotiator on this and we've walked away without a deal at the end of the day. Uh, and I think that that's extraordinary that this is the I mean that this hasn't really happened before. We've we've got to a stage where there's been no agreement. I think when Kevin Rudd was in Copenhagen back in 2009, was it, that there was no agreement, but to have no deal at all is quite extraordinary. I think that people would be rightly disappointed by that.
Host: Could any negotiator any negotiator have delivered a consensus when some countries are determined not to include references to phasing out of fossil fuels and others won't accept it the other way?
Jane Hume: Yeah, look, I mean, I think each country obviously is going to work in its own national interest and that should include Australia. For instance, we need now to make sure that we have refining capacity, uh, you know, fuel refining capacity. And so it's very hard for us to not consider that and that's a bipartisan agreement. It's very hard for us not to consider that when making negotiations. So you know, each country has to act in its own best interest. You do not enrich other nations by impoverishing others. Uh, but um, you know, finding a pathway through I think is really important. Clearly these negotiations have broken down.
Host: Has Chris Bowen failed?
Jane Hume: Well, I think on any measure you'd say, yes, he has. Not only has he failed in these negotiations as the lead negotiator, but he's also failed Australians at the time when he has spent $150 million just to be there, just to get this uh this presidency in the first place. Our energy prices have gone up. Our emissions have 
flatlined. I think that's kind of disappointing. He's really got a job to do at home. I would have much rather Chris Bowen was here at home fixing the problems we have here rather than over there failing to get a deal overseas.
Host: Let's talk about gas. How close is the coalition to reach an agreement with the government on passing legislation for the national gas reservation scheme?
Jane Hume: Yeah, we should be really clear, we want a gas reservation. We've been saying that from the start, but it can't be at any price. The government has moved a long way. I think the carve out of WA was a significant move and a good start, but there's more that can be done. We want to make sure that we get the calibration of this right. We can't afford an oversupply domestically that would have detrimental effects on uh on prices for investors. We need new gas in the system, more gas in the system, more investment in gas. And if we get this wrong, well then we will turn that gas investment away. It would be great to have that sugar hit of lower gas prices for manufacturers in the short and medium term, but if we can't get the investment in gas in the long term, well then we are doing consumers a massive disservice. We think we can get there. The government has moved. The government has shown a willingness to negotiate. I hope that we get there this week.
Host: Do you think you will?
Jane Hume: I I hope that we do, but it's really the the ball is in the government's court. It's we've been really clear on what it is that we want to see occur. Getting that calibration of domestic supply right is really important.
Host: The Greens are in negotiations about this as well. Uh do you risk leaving it to the Greens to finalize and not being able to influence the final shape of the scheme?
Jane Hume: I don't think business or indeed the labor government want to do a deal with the Greens on this one. They know what the Greens want is to shut down gas in Australia, not have a gas reservation that would is so desperately needed to make sure that we can maintain lower prices here and also increase gas supply in the future.
Host: You're listening to Radio National Breakfast. My guest is deputy leader of the Opposition, Jane Hume. When it comes to digital duty of care bill, the government also wants through Parliament this week, the government says it is changing its proposal to exempt some small businesses. The impact on small businesses was a key concern of the opposition. Does this address your concerns?
Jane Hume: No. No, it doesn't. I can't see a way through for the digital duty of care bill. And every time the government made says that it's made a step to amend it, it just seems to make the problem more worse. And look the fundamental problem remains. It's still a blank check check for censorship, particularly political censorship. It gives the government and the e-safety Commissioner sweeping powers over what are very vague and subjective definitions of what online harm is. Who decides what is harmful? And by whose values that is decided, I think should be of great concern to Australians. We of course, we want to see children protected online, and we've made that clear. That was what our social media ban was all about. The government's failed to deliver that policy. Maybe we should get that right before we start dealing in a a much broader policy that could essentially enable political censorship in a way that would be very detrimental to our democracy.
Host: Let's talk about AI. Foreign Minister Penny Wong is expected to elevate artificial intelligence as a major foreign policy and national security challenge in a major speech to Parliament tomorrow. Does the opposition agree that that's how AI should be viewed in the current context?
Jane Hume: AI is pervasive in all parts of our lives, whether it be employment, whether it be national security, whether it be defense and cyber security, or or just in our daily lives. We need to make sure that we can use this new technology, that we can embrace this new technology for our advantage, to drive productivity, to get better outcomes and create more opportunities, but at the same time, we have to make sure that we keep Australians safe and that we're acting in our national interest. That's why we've been so enthusiastic about this bipartisan uh um joint standing committee uh joint sorry, joint select committee on on AI. I think that's been working very well. I was talking to John O' Danium, who's uh our most senior shadow minister that's been on that committee just last night. He's been very pleased with the way that it's moving. There is going to be an interim report to that committee that's released this week. Uh there were a lot of bipartisan recommendations there. I think that people should feel very comfortable that the government and the opposition are working together in the national interest to make sure that we can take advantage of AI, but also protect ourselves from its harms.
Host: How urgently does Australia need to move when it comes to AI regulation?
Jane Hume: We have to move because if we don't move, we will simply be left behind. We want certainty with what it is that we are dealing with, but we don't want to overregulate it. We certainly don't want to see something as dangerous as a union writer veto over adoption of AI in the workplace, for instance. That would be a disaster because you cannot allow unions to dictate on the adoption of policies and the adoption of um of new technology in the workplace, particularly when workplaces are so inflexible now that just in order to keep businesses afloat, and there's 46 a day that are going under right now, just in order to keep themselves afloat, businesses have to adapt.
Host: Jane Hume, thank you for coming in.
Jane Hume: Great to be with you, Sally.
